title: Entry 1: df2 Data Cleaning — Case, Spacing, and Missing Data
text:
This exercise cleaned a student data set across three columns: name, final_score, and passed. Rather than treating every missing value the same way, I worked through each column individually and documented the reasoning behind each decision, using both base R and tidyverse approaches.
# preview the raw, uncleaned data
df2

   student_id  name final_score passed
1         101   Ava          88    yes
2         102  Noah          NA     no
3         103  <NA>          92   <NA>
4         104   mia          75    yes
5         105   Leo          81    yes
6         106   Zoe          NA     no
7         107  <NA>          84   <NA>
8         108   Eli          90    yes
9         109 chloe          NA     no
10        110   sam          86    yes
# data inspection
str(df2)

'data.frame':   10 obs. of  4 variables:
 $ student_id : int  101 102 103 104 105 106 107 108 109 110
 $ name       : chr  "Ava" "Noah" NA "mia" ...
 $ final_score: num  88 NA 92 75 81 NA 84 90 NA 86
 $ passed     : chr  "yes" "no" NA "yes" ...

colSums(is.na(df2))

 student_id        name final_score      passed 
          0           2           3           2

title: Entry 1: df2 Data Cleaning — Case, Spacing, and Missing Data
text:
Base R Version

Cleaning: “name” — Case and Spacing, Missing Values Left As-Is

unique(df2$name)

[1] "Ava"   "Noah"  NA      "mia"   "Leo"   "Zoe"   "Eli"   "chloe" "sam"  

unique(trimws(df2$name)) #checks for space inconsistencies 

[1] "Ava"   "Noah"  NA      "mia"   "Leo"   "Zoe"   "Eli"   "chloe" "sam"  

df2$name <- trimws(df2$name) #removes the white space
df2$name <- str_to_title(df2$name) #convert all names to title case
#Verify that it worked
unique(df2$name)

[1] "Ava"   "Noah"  NA      "Mia"   "Leo"   "Zoe"   "Eli"   "Chloe" "Sam"  


Decision: name left as NA (2 missing values)
Decision: name left as NA (2 missing values)
Rationale: name functions as an identifier, but it cannot be reasonably estimated. There is no representative “average” or “typical” name to impute, unlike a numeric column. A placeholder was considered but rejected, since it would add no analytical value here. Because student_id is complete with no missing values, every row, including these two, remains fully identifiable and traceable by ID, even without a name. Leaving name as NA preserves the row’s other valid data (score, passed) while staying transparent that the name specifically was not recorded.
Limitation: any results reporting a person’s name (for example, who had the top score) should note that 2 respondents cannot be identified by name, though they remain identifiable by student_id.


Cleaning: “final_score” — Imputation

#Clean the final_score column removing the missing values and replace with zero
df2$final_score[is.na(df2$final_score)] <- 0
#verify that it worked
df2$final_score

 [1] 88  0 92 75 81  0 84 90  0 86

sum(is.na(df2$final_score))

[1] 0

df2

   student_id  name final_score passed
1         101   Ava          88    yes
2         102  Noah           0     no
3         103  <NA>          92   <NA>
4         104   Mia          75    yes
5         105   Leo          81    yes
6         106   Zoe           0     no
7         107  <NA>          84   <NA>
8         108   Eli          90    yes
9         109 Chloe           0     no
10        110   Sam          86    yes


Note: after reviewing all parts of the data frame, information from the passed column was used to determine that replacing NA with zero was a sound decision, given that the student did not pass.


Cleaning: “passed” — Case and Missing Values

unique(df2$passed)

[1] "yes" "no"  NA   

unique(trimws(df2$passed))  #checks for spacing inconsistencies 

[1] "yes" "no"  NA   

df2$passed <-trimws(df2$passed) #removes the white spaces
df2$passed <- str_to_title(df2$passed) #convert all names to title case
df2$passed[is.na(df2$passed)] <- "yes" 
#verify that it worked
df2$passed

 [1] "Yes" "No"  "yes" "Yes" "Yes" "No"  "yes" "Yes" "No"  "Yes"

sum(is.na(df2$passed))

[1] 0

2         102  Noah           0     No
3         103  <NA>          92    yes
4         104   Mia          75    Yes
5         105   Leo          81    Yes
6         106   Zoe           0     No

9         109 Chloe           0     No

Note: after reviewing all parts of the data frame, information from the final_score column was used to predict and apply “yes” to the passed column based on the score.

title: Entry 1: df2 Data Cleaning — Case, Spacing, and Missing Data
text:
What this showed me:
Cleaning this dataset made clear that missing values don’t all deserve the same treatment. A missing name has no reasonable estimate. There’s no “typical” name to fall back on, so it was left as NA and documented as a limitation. But final_score and passed could actually inform each other: knowing a student’s outcome (passed = no) supported treating a missing score as 0, and knowing the score supported inferring the outcome where passed was missing. Making that connection between columns, rather than treating each one in isolation, was the more meaningful decision here than the mechanics of the cleaning code itself.

title: Entry 1: df2 Data Cleaning — Case, Spacing, and Missing Data
text:
Tidyverse Version
To compare approaches, I repeated the same exercise using tidyverse syntax instead of base R.

Cleaning: “name” — Case and Spacing, Missing Values Left As-Is

unique(df2$name) #view the unique values

[1] "Ava"   "Noah"  NA      "Mia"   "Leo"   "Zoe"   "Eli"   "Chloe" "Sam"

[1] "Ava"   "Noah"  NA      "Mia"   "Leo"   "Zoe"   "Eli"   "Chloe" "Sam"  

df2$name <- df2$name %>%  # now correct case and spacing
  trimws() %>%
  str_to_title()
#verify that it worked
unique(df2$name)

[1] "Ava"   "Noah"  NA      "Mia"   "Leo"   "Zoe"   "Eli"   "Chloe" "Sam"  


Note: name is left as NA, for the same reasoning documented in the base R version above.

  mutate(final_score = replace_na(final_score, 0)) #imputation with 0

title: My Journey
text:
Hi, I’m Gyna.


Change is inevitable. As the world is changing to include AI - well, in this case it is already incorporated into our day-to-day lives and our work environments. And honestly, I’m here for it. I welcome the positive benefits that artificial intelligence contributes to the betterment of society and the human condition. Thus, after careful introspection of the best ways to use my knowledge and talent of human capital, business acumen, and pattern recognition; I pledge to collect and interpret data in a socially responsible way.



Research is not necessarily new to me but I took for granted the impact data collection has on decision making at both the micro and macro levels. Understanding that data collection - rather the interpretation of collected data is the catalyst that shapes commerce, marketing, and social policy; it’s the driving force of how goods and services are now being rendered to the everyday person.



This website is a reintroduction of research and data analysis but also a real time pivot in my career from direct implementation of services to provide direction for staff, identify gaps in training, and deliver service based outcomes, using tools such as R, SQL and Quarto. Learning data analysis using synthetic databases allows me to showcase the reasoning behind each decision, documented as I rebuild the skill from the ground up.

My background is in sociology and HR-adjacent work. You can read more about that path on the My Journey page. This site itself is focused on the work: browse Learning Progress to see what I’ve built so far and visit the Blog for my thoughts on real-world topics and my response to current events.

title: Entry 2: Survey Data Cleaning — RespondentID, Age_Group, Satisfaction, and Would_Recommend
text:
What this showed me:
Partway through cleaning the Would_Recommend column, I noticed I kept creating a new, separately labeled variable at every single step instead of building on the version I had just cleaned. It worked, but it was harder to follow and not actually necessary. Once I recognized that, I pivoted to cleaning one column progressively: trimming spacing, then building directly on that result to fix case, then building on that result again to handle missing values, instead of relabeling at every step. That shift made the logic easier to follow and set up the same thinking I needed for writing clean pipe chains in tidyverse.
I also learned an important distinction while cleaning RespondentID: removing values, like missing data or duplicates, is different from transforming values, like trimming or changing case. A transformation can be assigned back into a single column, but removing entries actually removes whole rows, so the result has to be assigned back into the full data frame, not just one column, since every column in a data frame has to stay the same length.

title: What Do These “isms” Mean?
text:
Revisting Capitalism, Socialism, and Fascism
Words by Gyna Jones

2026-10-19
Revisiting Capitalism, Socialism, and Fascism
What Do These “isms” Mean?
Revisiting Capitalism, Socialism, and Fascism
It’s that time again: elections. With the upcoming elections, parties positions and their ideologies take center stage. Early voting will commence as early as Oct 13th in some states until November 3rd, 2026. And make no mistake, the terms Capitalism, Socialism, and Fascism will be on the minds of many voters as they decide who to cast their vote for. These terms have been buzzwords in the news, on campaign trails, and on social media. But what do these “isms” really mean? And will these ideologies impact the way people intend to vote. In “Guides to the Political Conflicts”: Donald Lazere defines Capitalism, Socialism, and Fascism as the following.

title: What Do These “isms” Mean?
text:
Capitalism
Capitalism – is an economy based on profit-seeking investments and resources obtained through labor of its productive population. The return on investments and resource management are the results of excess wealth and or poverty. This economic structure can be adapted alongside democracy, plutocracy, fascism, and even a dictatorship (286).

title: What Do These “isms” Mean?
text:
Socialism
Socialism - is an economic structure that functions on the idea that resources of the productive majority go directly to meet the needs of its people.Infrastructure and industry are governed by federal, state, and local governments, workers, and community members. This economic system can be adapted to both a democratic and or communist government (286).

title: What Do These “isms” Mean?
text:
Fascism
Fascism – is an economic system based on private industry and state capitalism. This centralization of wealth and resources are the results of maintaining a ruling class and absolute power. This economic structure cannot be adapted to democracy and thrives under a dictatorship or communistic government (287).

title: What Do These “isms” Mean?
text:
Conclusion
While these are just definitions of much deeper concepts, each, when implemented, has had lasting consequences when executed as an economic and or governing system. How will we vote? While that is a private decision, it is also our civil duty to become well versed in the history, the impact and the relevance to current events when these types of buzz words are used in an election year. Knowing this prepares one to recognize which candidate(s) or party aligns with individual values but more importantly the country as a whole.
Kalb, Don, and Walden Bello. “Blacklash”: The Global Rise of the Radical Right,Pulto Press, 2026.https://doi.org/10.2307/jj.33676682.
Lazere, Donald. “Guides to the Political Conflicts”. Writing and Reading Across the Curriculum, edited by Laurence Behrens and Leonard J. Rosen., 6th ed., Addison Wesley Longman, 1997, pp. 282-289.
Wright, Erik Olin.”Social Empowerment of Socialism.” Berkeley Journal of Sociology, Vol, 50, 2006, pp. 147-167.
